plan.working_title: Stopping a GLP-1: What Slowed Weight Regain in a New Trial #shorts
plan.why: A permanent high-search question with a fresh Oct 7 RCT hook. The radar marked it caution, so the angle stays trial-data-only. | fact-check: I confirmed the pilot: Hollis-Hansen et al., 'Preventing Weight Regain After GLP-1 Therapy Discontinuation: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial', Obesity Science & Practice 2026 (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/osp4.70194). It randomized 39 adults: 14 to usual care, 12 to the app and 13 to medically tailored meals. Estimated 4-month regain was 10.75% with usual care, 3.60% with the app and 3.58% with the meals. Weight was an EXPLORATORY outcome. The primary outcome was adherence and satisfaction, so 'slowed' must be hedged. For the opening, STEP 1's extension (Wilding et al., 2022, Diabetes Obes Metab) found that a subset of STEP 1 adults regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within 1 year of stopping. Keep it to that population. Avoid any framing that suggests stopping is a safe plan.

Stopping a GLP-1? Here's what a small trial found might help 📉

A few things worth knowing:
• In the STEP 1 extension, adults without diabetes who stopped semaglutide and the trial's lifestyle program regained about two-thirds of their lost weight within a year.
• A new pilot trial randomized 39 adults coming off a GLP-1 to usual care, an app, or medically tailored meals.

factcheck.summary: The claims check out against the sources. STEP 1 extension (Wilding et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2022): one year after stopping semaglutide 2.4 mg and the trial's lifestyle program, participants "regained two-thirds of their prior weight loss." Hollis-Hansen et al. pilot RCT (Obesity Science & Practice, Oct 2026, 12(5), PMC13643368): 39 adults within 30 days of stopping a GLP-1, split into usual care (n=14), the Noom app (n=12) and medically tailored meals (n=13) for 4 months. Primary outcomes were adherence and satisfaction, and weight change was explicitly called "exploratory." Estimated gain was 10.75% for control (95% CI 7.03–14.47), 3.60% for the app (p=0.007) and 3.58% for the meals (p=0.006). "Roughly a third as much" is right (3.6/10.75 ≈ 0.33). The authors say the trial was "not powered for definitive efficacy testing" and call for larger trials. The script's caveat, its "linked to" wording, its prescriber framing and its avoidance of the app's brand name are all appropriate. It contains no stopping or switching advice. At about 141 words it is well within the Shorts limit. There are only minor clarity fixes, listed below.

issues.claim: Estimated regain was 10.75% with usual care, versus about 3.6% with either the app or the meals.
issues.problem: s2 says 'two-thirds of lost weight' (a share of the weight lost), but the pilot's figures are percent of body weight gained since stopping. Viewers could read 10.75% as 10.75% of the weight they had lost. The two units sit next to each other and are never told apart.
issues.fix: Narration: "Estimated gain was 10.75% of body weight with usual care, versus about 3.6% with either the app or the meals. Roughly a third as much." stat_label: "Estimated 4-month weight gain (% of body weight): support vs usual care"

issues.claim: this pilot randomized 39 adults coming off a GLP-1
issues.problem: Accurate. Only 34 of 39 had a final weigh-in, and participants were enrolled within 30 days of stopping. This is optional context, not an error.
issues.fix: Optional: on-screen text "Pilot: 39 adults, 4 months (34 with final weigh-in)". Keep the narration as written.

issues.claim: adults who stopped semaglutide and the trial's lifestyle program regained about two-thirds of their lost weight within 1 year
issues.problem: Accurate. The extension was a subset of STEP 1 (adults with obesity or overweight, without diabetes). Leaving out the population is acceptable for a Short.
issues.fix: Optional: "in the STEP 1 extension, adults without diabetes who stopped semaglutide and the trial's lifestyle program regained about two-thirds of their lost weight within 1 year."
